limit: No published study measures how often a street harasser does one particular thing after one particular response. A number below is copied from the cited page. Where no number exists, the entry says so.
promptBrief: Research, not a script, and you still only speak the stance you were given. Most men who do this open with a greeting, a request for a name or a minute, or telling her to smile, because they say they wanted a friendly reaction. A short calm no is not flirting: answer the no. Being ignored is sometimes met with anger at being ignored. An insult is the response most likely to draw anger back. A bystander stepping in beside a calm firm no is the pattern associated with him leaving. A camera alone rarely ends it; he may tell them to put the phone down. When the stance is leaving, save face and go. Never invent a statistic, a slur, or anything sexual.
firmBystanderRule: A calm firm boundary with a bystander makes him back off. Cornell found New York incidents more likely to stop when a bystander confronted the harasser, and Stop Street Harassment says a short no can be effective. No study gives a rate for the combination.

rtb_direct_caution.title: What to do if you see sexual assault or harassment (summarises Right To Be's caution on Direct)

behaviors.text: In a 2,000-person nationally representative GfK survey, 65% of women in the United States had experienced at least one type of street harassment. 57% of all women had experienced verbal harassment and 41% a physically aggressive form, including sexual touching (23%) and following (20%).
The same survey: being harassed by one man was the most common experience for women (70%). 38% of women had been harassed by two or more men. Respondents could choose more than one.

The report's examples of what street harassment sounds like, at the non-explicit end, are honking or whistling, an uninvited greeting, being told to smile, and a request for a name, number, or date that continues after a no.

About 22% of all women in that survey had been called a sexist slur such as 'bitch' or 'slut' by a stranger in public. The simulation allows a crude insult only in a hostile stance and never a slur about race, religion, disability, or orientation.
68% of harassed women in the US survey were very or somewhat concerned the incident would escalate. 25% were very concerned. That is fear, not a measurement of how often escalation happens.

More than 16,600 women answered the 2014 Hollaback! survey led at Cornell. The school's summary of findings from 22 countries says more than half of respondents had been groped or fondled by a street harasser.

UN Women's Safe Cities report: a Rabat study found 92% of women had experienced some form of sexual harassment in their lifetime. Quito's 2011 scoping study found 68% of women had experienced some form of sexual violence in public spaces in the previous year. In Port Moresby, more than half of women market vendors had experienced some form of violence in the markets.

responses.text: The most common proactive response in the US survey was telling a harasser to stop or back off (31% of all women). The report says a simple 'no', 'back off', or 'stop harassing me' can be effective. No study measures how often a firm no ends a street encounter or draws hostility.
phrasing: repeats her no as if it were an overreaction
insists he was only being friendly
does not answer as if she had flirted

responses.text: Focus groups in the same report describe men turning angry or insulting after being ignored, including demanding to know why she was ignoring them. These are accounts, not rates. Staying silent does not mean the remark does not happen.
phrasing: asks why she will not answer
takes the silence as an insult
does not invent words she did not say

responses.text: In 223 New York incidents submitted to Hollaback!, bystanders were present in 31%. Where they were present, the report says they had a positive effect 26% of the time, a negative effect 22% of the time, and took no action 19% of the time. When a bystander confronted the harasser, the harassment was more likely to cease. The report gives no percentage for that last finding. A knowing look or an empathetic remark could be enough to help the woman.
phrasing: notices he is no longer alone with her
save-face remark and leaves when the stance is back_off
may turn on the bystander when the stance says so

responses.text: Right To Be says to record only when someone else is already helping, and to let the person who was harassed decide what happens to the footage. Filming by itself is not described as what stops the incident. No study gives a rate for how harassers react to a camera.
phrasing: tells them to put the phone down
does not invent a threat of violence

responses.text: The US report's focus groups include men answering a short refusal with an insult. Practitioner guidance treats losing one's temper as the risky response. There is no measured increase in risk.
phrasing: answers the insult with wounded pride
stays inside a crude insult, not a slur or a sexual threat

fiveDs.name: Distract
fiveDs.text: Ignore the person harassing and talk to the person being harassed about something unrelated, or get in the way. Four of the five Ds are indirect and are meant not to escalate.

fiveDs.name: Delegate
fiveDs.text: Ask a third person to help, and say clearly what you see and what you want them to do. A shop worker, driver, or the person next to you can be the delegate.

fiveDs.name: Document
fiveDs.text: Record or take notes only if someone else is already helping and you are safe. Ask the person who was harassed what to do with the recording. Do not post it without permission.

fiveDs.name: Delay
fiveDs.text: If you could not act in the moment, check in afterwards. Ask if she is okay, say that what happened was not acceptable, and offer practical company.

fiveDs.name: Direct
fiveDs.text: Name the behaviour or tell him to stop, briefly. Right To Be treats Direct as the risky one: he may turn on you or escalate. Use it only if you and she are physically safe, escalation looks unlikely, and she seems to want someone to speak.

noRightResponse.text: Right To Be's guide is the 5Ds, and the US survey is explicit that telling him to stop is common, not that any one response controls him. There is no measured 'correct' reply. Source: Stop Street Harassment, 2014 national report, https://stopstreetharassment.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/2014-National-SSH-Street-Harassment-Report.pdf

firmBoundary.text: Telling him to stop or back off was the most common proactive response in that survey (31% of women). The report says a short 'no' can be effective. It does not say how often he then leaves. Source: https://stopstreetharassment.org/our-work/nationalstudy/2014study/

fiveDCitation.text: These five are Right To Be's 5Ds (formerly Hollaback!): Distract, Delegate, Document, Delay, Direct. Four are indirect. Direct is the one they tell you to use with caution. https://righttobe.org/guides/bystander-intervention-training/

bystanderStops.text: In the Cornell and Hollaback! review of 223 New York incidents, harassment was more likely to cease when a bystander confronted the harasser. The report gives no percentage. https://www.ilr.cornell.edu/sites/default/files-d8/ILR_Report_TARGET_1B_11202012_1.pdf
